items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: Like Charlie Parker. All alto players sound like Charlie Parker.

ctx.x: How do you feel about that? How did that effect the music? Do you think it was a —

Oh, it had its toll on jazz because there are no more big bands, there are I think only the Count Basie Band and the Duke Ellington Band, but it’s not like the leader was there, like if you cut the head of a snake off, the tail dies, and the head of the snake was like the band leader, like Count Basie. The big bands were so popular in those days, until, and they, most of the musicians in those days demanded respect because they were an artist. And they were all individualists. Everybody had a sound of their own. They could be identified on the record like if Billie Holiday would sing on the record you’d know it’s nobody but Billie Holiday. items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I like Charlie Parker. I could understand what Charlie Parker’s doing. ‘Cause he could play, he could swing, oh, he was mean.

ctx.x: You got that right. You make the notes count as you get older. Like Dizzy used to say, his chops ain’t what they used to be, and he doesn’t get ahold of that horn like he used to. I said, “Well, I told you a long time, Birks, you know, as you get older, you’re going to have to slow down.” And you know it does, you slow down. I never have wanted to play fast, dazzle as you say, with your ability to get over your horn, because guys wasn’t doing it when I was coming up. Louis Armstrong, he wasn’t dazzling anybody…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: He was playing like Charlie Parker even before Charlie Parker even thought there was a style he was playing. Bird used to go around and listen to him...

ctx.x: Well, had you given him any trouble or --

No. Well, Charlie and Rama had played with Dizzy so they wanted somebody in the band that they had played with. You know, they were good buddies. And I'm from St. Louis, you know. But Dizzy and I got in a little -- we started playing some "Body and Soul" in a place in Philadelphia one night and I kind of made a little noise that night, playing "Body and Soul." So Lucky hired me back. And Dizzy went with Teddy Hill. Come the side 3 - end

But after we went from Philadelphia back to New York, that's when Bobby Moore took ill and I -- Herschel and Jo, they recommended me to Basie and I took his place, you know. And -- oh, that was the latter part of 1937. But I still wanted to learn more about music because when I joined Basie's band, it was nothing but head arrangements. Everything was head arrangements. They didn't have -- I bet they didn't have 10 manuscripts, you know.

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: And, you know, you take the Charlie Parkers and the Fats Navarros and the guys like that, they sat down and they played.

ctx.x: And he had something to deviate his mind from the drugs to dancing. And he got his exercise.

And, you know, you take the Charlie Parkers and the Fats Navarros and the guys like that, they sat down and they played. Well, Ray Nance, you know, he would get up, he would do his dance, he would sing, you know.
But another thing about him, you never saw him nodding off. Not like --
